#5866. A State Law Targeted Fentanyl Dealers. Prosecutors Are Using It to Charge Users Too.

— More than 30 people in Idaho have been charged with fentanyl trafficking without proof of sales

When two Idaho lawmakers pitched harsher penalties for people caught with fentanyl, they said the new law would target drug dealers -- not those struggling with addiction.

But 2 years after the law was implemented, prosecutors have charged at least 30 people with fentanyl trafficking without presenting evidence that they were dealing or distributing the drug.

The law, which went into effect on July 1, 2024, does not differentiate between those using and those selling the drug, and it doesn't require prosecutors to find evidence of trafficking. Instead, prosecutors can charge people with fentanyl trafficking if they possess at least 4 grams or 100 pills that contain fentanyl. InvestigateWest reviewed court records for all fentanyl trafficking charges filed through June 30 of this year. Among the 90 cases that included arrest reports, one-third of them lacked evidence such as scales, ledgers, and small bags, which when found together are commonly considered proof that someone sold or intended to sell drugs. But court records show those people were charged with trafficking and face the law's mandatory minimum prison terms based on the amount of fentanyl police said they had.

A sheriff deputy in western Idaho's Nez Perce County arrested a man for drug possession after he dropped a bag of blue pills that the deputy identified as fentanyl on the floor of a casino, according to the police report. After counting 111 pills, "I changed the charge from possession, to trafficking fentanyl," the deputy wrote in the report.

One county north, Isaac Berger was charged with fentanyl trafficking by the Latah County Prosecutor's Office after an emergency room nurse who was treating him for an overdose reported Berger to police. Less than 3 months later, Berger died of fentanyl poisoning. The detective who investigated Berger's death said there was no evidence that he was planning to sell or distribute the drugs, which Berger's mother brought to the hospital in an effort to help healthcare workers save her son.

Prosecutors who supported the law during legislative debates continue to defend it, saying it deters drug dealers from bringing fentanyl into the state, though none provided evidence to support the claim. Fifteen people charged with trafficking fentanyl were accused by police of selling drugs to an informant or admitting they sold drugs. Seven of them were convicted and are serving time in prison.

"Treatment is not the right outcome for every case," Bonneville County Prosecuting Attorney Randy Neal said. "Accountability is just as important. And if you're looking at somebody who's distributing, who's delivering, if you don't have the accountability, I promise you, probation is a joke."

Neal, who has been a vocal advocate of the law, pointed to a graphic originating from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration widely shared by prosecutors and law enforcement showing a No. 2 pencil with 2 mg of fentanyl powder on the tip, which can be lethal. Neal said "it's highly unlikely" that someone caught with the state threshold of at least 4 grams -- about four sugar packets -- of fentanyl is not planning to distribute it "because the numbers are so insane."

Opponents of Idaho's law disagree. Kellen Russoniello, MPH, director of public health for the Drug Policy Alliance, which advocates for drug treatment instead of criminalization, said it would not be unusual for someone with a severe addiction and a higher tolerance, or someone who made a bulk purchase on payday, to acquire the state's 4-gram threshold.

Russoniello said state lawmakers could save lives by diverting more people to treatment. InvestigateWest's analysis revealed that 13 people charged with trafficking received substance use treatment instead of prison. (All of them accepted plea deals for a different charge. The law's mandatory minimum prison terms do not allow for alternative sentences.) Forty people have served time in prison after being convicted of the trafficking charge or pleading guilty to an alternative charge.

"This law is ensnaring people who are possessing for personal use," Russoniello said. "Prosecuting or imprisoning people instead of providing necessary health services is counterproductive, ultimately making recovery more difficult by compounding trauma and saddling people with criminal records that will make accessing housing, employment, and services more difficult."

Republican state legislators Rep. Ted Hill and Sen. Todd Lakey introduced the law at a January 2024 hearing. Fentanyl possession and intent to deliver were already felonies with the possibility of prison -- a decision that was typically made by judges.

But House Bill 406 added a new trafficking offense that allows people in possession of threshold amounts of fentanyl to be charged as traffickers and imposes mandatory prison terms of 3, 5, or 10 years depending on the amount. The lawmakers, who represent constituents in and near Ada County, the state's most populated county, said the change was needed to "shut down the cartels" and prevent rising overdose deaths. Fentanyl-related deaths spiked in Idaho in 2021 and reached their highest point in 2023, when the drug killed 197 people, according to data from the state Department of Health and Welfare. Each year, fentanyl was responsible for more overdose deaths than any other drug, the data show.

By the time the fentanyl trafficking law went into effect in 2024, deaths had begun to decline. Last year saw the same number of fatalities as 2024, according to the data. (Lakey and Hill did not respond to calls and messages from InvestigateWest for this article.)

Idaho is one of nine states that allows people to be charged as traffickers based on possession above a certain threshold, according to a 2025 report by the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association summarizing fentanyl criminal statutes by state. Idaho's threshold is similar to other states, but it is the only state allowing pill counts to be used instead of grams. Seven of those states, including Idaho, have mandatory minimum prison terms.

Two years after Idaho's law took effect, prosecutors across the state have charged 134 people with fentanyl trafficking, InvestigateWest's analysis of court records found. Thirty-one of those cases are still pending.

Of the completed cases, 30% were dismissed and nearly half resulted in plea deals for other charges, such as possession of a controlled substance or possession with intent to deliver. Twenty-two people were convicted of fentanyl trafficking and are serving time in prison.

When attorney Mike French opposed the law on behalf of the Idaho Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers during a legislative debate, she said it's drug users, not traffickers, who are getting caught up in the state's mandatory minimum laws for marijuana, cocaine, and heroin trafficking. Laws like this do not effectively deter people struggling with addiction, she said, because they're typically unaware of the potential criminal penalties or are unable to stop using without help.

"This is a sledge hammer when we need a scalpel," French said.

Idaho's fentanyl trafficking law continued a decades-long trend where state lawmakers have sought to curb drug use by sharpening criminal penalties, despite national research showing those penalties do not deter drug use. A 10-year-old U.S. Department of Justice report found that "increasing the severity of punishment does little to deter crime."

The most effective response combines law enforcement efforts that target traffickers and alternatives to prison for people who are using but not selling drugs, according to a 2018 Pew Center report titled "More Imprisonment Does Not Reduce State Drug Problems." Drug courts, community supervision, and reduced prison sentences for drug offenders in Oklahoma, Mississippi, Alaska, and other states decreased prison populations and the cost to taxpayers in those states, the Pew Center found.

Russoniello, public health director at the Drug Policy Alliance, said lawmakers across the country are in "a moment where the pendulum is swinging back towards tough-on-crime and the war-on-drugs mentality."

Policies like Idaho's, which allow prosecutors to charge crimes like trafficking without any evidence of trafficking or intent to sell, circumvent well-established rights granted to people entangled in the criminal justice system, Russoniello said.

Families Against Mandatory Minimums, whose founder launched the nonprofit after her brother was sentenced to 5 years in prison for a drug crime, calls the practice "unjust, irrational, or counterproductive." Katrina Baugh, the nonprofit's national policy director, said mandatory incarceration allows increased political influence in courtrooms, by letting lawmakers and prosecutors rather than courts dictate criminal punishments. Mandatory minimum prison terms strip judges of discretion in sentencing, shifting the decision "away from the impartial adjudicator," she said, giving the power instead to "the party that has a self-interest of pursuing harsher punishments in every case."

Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Bill Thompson, who charged Berger after his nurse called police, said limiting judicial discretion was necessary because some judges were not coming down hard enough on drug dealers.

"Historically, in our part of the state, our judges have not been particularly strong on what we consider to be appropriate punishments for people who actually are dealing the drugs, not just users," Thompson said. "So the trafficking statutes have been a really important tool in trying to get around that reluctance that we encounter on occasion with some members of the courts."

Berger was the first person in Latah County to be charged under the new law. He was arrested at a hospital in the university town of Moscow in May 2025 and taken to jail. Berger and his attorney were working on a treatment plan they hoped would result in reduced charges. But Berger's health rapidly declined, and he died at home 2 months later from fentanyl poisoning – one of two Idahoans who fatally overdosed while their case was pending.

Fentanyl trafficking charges have been filed by prosecutors in 18 of Idaho's 44 counties. Six counties account for more than 75% of the charges.

In eastern Idaho near the Wyoming border, prosecutor Neal's office in Bonneville County has filed 28 charges -- more than any other county. One person was convicted of the charge. Sixteen others accepted plea deals for other charges including possession and delivering a controlled substance. Interstate 15, which runs from northern Montana to Southern California, cuts through the county and is a known drug pipeline, Neal said. He also credits a drug task force that's a collaboration between the county sheriff's department and Idaho Falls police with successful arrests and prosecutions.

"The effectiveness of the law enforcement is what you're seeing the numbers reflect," Neal said when presented with InvestigateWest's findings. "So, if our folks in Idaho Falls have a special drug task force, and a place like Rigby doesn't have a task force or doesn't have a specialized unit, well, that's going to skew the numbers because it's going to look like Bonneville has a hell of a lot bigger drug problem than Jefferson County. It's just that Jefferson's making less arrests."

Major thoroughfares that are known routes for transporting drugs between states also cut through Bannock, Kootenai, and Shoshone counties, accounting for some of the charges filed by prosecutors there. At least seven of those arrests originated from traffic stops, court records show. Meanwhile, in Ada and Canyon counties, which have the state's densest populations, more crime resulted in more charges.

Charges in Ada County, which encompasses Boise, resulted in more fentanyl trafficking convictions than anywhere else. The Ada County Prosecutor's Office, run by Jan Bennetts, who was elected to the position in 2016, declined requests for an interview. Alyson Outen, a spokesperson for the office, said in an email that the law "was a needed change."

Multiple overdoses had been reported at Andrea Forbini's home in Boise by the time police showed up with a search warrant in May 2025, according to court documents. They found nearly 400 pills containing fentanyl and arrested Forbini and two of her roommates, police records show. Only Forbini was charged with trafficking fentanyl.

Forbini's daughter, Halle Lillquist, said her mother struggled with addiction for most of her life, leaning on drugs to treat the pain she experienced from autoimmune conditions. She had recovered from an overdose weeks before being arrested last year. Over Lillquist's objections, Forbini's boyfriend bailed her mom out of jail, Lillquist said.

"Jail was just detox," Lillquist said. "She wasn't getting treatment there but at least she was sober."

Lillquist said she understands the need to punish people like her mom, who have committed a crime. But in states like Idaho that increase penalties without addressing the addiction, nothing will change.

Jail kept Forbini sober for about 3 months, but without addiction treatment she relapsed after her release, Lillquist said. One week later, her mom died from fentanyl poisoning.

"They shouldn't have let her go so freely like that without any help," Lillquist said. "Something should have been done."

#5865. Thermal Dawn — Thermal Storage Is Cheap Storage

Another great idea from Down Under: Thermal Dawn promises cost effective heating and cooling, mainly by replacing gas boilers in cold climates. CleanTechnica had a chance to interview Nick Zeniou, Founder of Thermal Dawn, recently by phone, fresh after his presentation at Everything Electric. You can hear him explain his revolutionary system here, or here with a little less drama.

Everything Electric was a good opportunity to measure public reaction to the new product. Nick tells me that hundreds of people checked out their stall. “People care about carbon cost and comfort. People don’t compromise on comfort.” Sounds like comfort trumps carbon cost. Homeowners who visited the stand and filled out the survey were focused on sustainability and cost. Nick cautions: “it was an electrification expo crowd, and 50 of the 62 already had solar, so it’s not the whole market.” See the chart below.

Although I live in the warmer part of Australia (Brisbane), many Aussies have to endure cold winters. Nick tells me he is looking at installs in Sydney, Canberra, and Melbourne in the deep south. Thermal Dawn can store heat up to 70 degrees Celsius, or down to 5 degrees. Thermal Dawns’ equipment can run cold or hot water through pipes and radiators that are already installed, depending on the need — without having to run an expensive gas boiler. He describes it as a thermal battery. Just to be clear, it does not generate electricity.

Check out this graph below, which shows the Thermal Dawn system in action at a house in Melbourne during a day in August 2026. It shows room temperature and when the heat pump was running, in 15-minute samples, unedited. The heat pump ran until about 1:45pm, then not again, heated by stored energy through the evening peak.

“What about return on investment,” I asked. He described two systems they have had running over the southern Australian winter which have saved the homeowners approximately AU$1,500 each. “The first was a house in Melbourne, our first install, live since May 2026. The owners charge the system in their retailer’s free three-hour midday window, so the heat for the evening costs them close to nothing. The second was a Warragul (slab-heated home, Victoria): installed in two days in July 2026. Our controls turn the home’s concrete slab into part of the battery, managing when it charges and when it releases heat. On 95% of winter evenings, the heat pumps did not run at all between 5 pm and 9pm. Since commissioning, 70,521 MJ of gas has been avoided by just these two installations.”

Nick further explains: “A standard heat pump draws from the grid during those expensive morning and evening hours. You’ve escaped gas, but you’re still paying premium rates every time the temperature drops at night. Thermal Dawn is different. Our system charges when power is cheapest, a free midday window, your own solar, or late-night off-peak, then delivers that stored warmth through your radiators and underfloor heating all evening, with the compressor off through the expensive hours.

It appears that Thermal Dawn’s secret sauce is “Phase Change Materials.” Naturally, Nick declined to share exactly what Thermal Dawn is using. The system replaces a gas boiler with a combination of reverse cycle heat pump, well insulated water tank, and phase change materials. PCMs are designed to freeze or melt at a specific temperature, storing and releasing heat when they change physical state, usually from solid to liquid. “PCM doubles our heat capacity.” The heating applications I could understand, what about the cooling? “Cool water from the tank runs through a fan coil unit, and the fan blows cool air into the room. Cooling is an optional add-on.” That’s the answer.

How do thermal storage and a home battery/solar system work together? “Thermal storage is cheap storage doing one job very well. Heating, cooling, and hot water are the largest, most predictable loads in the house, and covering them thermally is far cheaper per kWh than covering them from lithium. A battery is expensive storage doing a general-purpose job.

“The practical effect is that your battery stops being the thing that carries your heating. It’s freed up for lights, appliances, the EV, and overnight backup, and it lasts longer for not being cycled hard every winter evening. Homes with a battery already are often the clearest case, because the expensive storage stops being spent on the cheapest possible job.”

Thermal dawn connects to existing hydronic pipework. The gas boiler with its high gas bills is gone. Check out the animation of heat discharge overnight. “The thermal battery charged on solar during the day and now heats the house while the heat pump stays off. It’s an illustration of what the app shows, not a recording of a live home.” For those rooms that don’t have hydronic radiators or underfloor slab heating, Thermal Dawn installs fan coil units. Nick tells me via a followup email that: “It’s a small indoor unit with a water coil and a fan: warm water from the thermal battery runs through the coil, and the fan blows the heating or cooling into the room.”

The heavy technical discussion out of the way, I asked Nick about his background. He grew up in an isolated part of New Zealand. His job was to collect the firewood for the family’s heat source — a fireplace. He had to get the fire going by 4:00 pm or the house would not warm up for the cold evening. Timing was very important, as it is for electricity use.

Nick is a mechanical engineer who has worked across tech companies and startups. While working on installing commercial air conditioning, he came across the idea that became Thermal Dawn. Nick joined the dots between the huge variations in electricity supply cost throughout each 24-hour period, with an average home’s thermal energy needs (up to two-thirds of consumption) and the fact that homes are becoming power stations. Thence to thermal batteries powered by Thermal Dawn technology.

He reminisces about the start of the business: “When our first unit was finished, we loaded it into a ute at 5pm and I drove it down the Hume overnight, Sydney to Melbourne (1000 km), to install it the next morning. We had a four-month-old at home at the time. My wife Linda is my co-founder and leads mechanical design and manufacturing, so while I was on the road, she was looking after a newborn.”

For those who would like to get involved, Nick invites Australian homeowners to sign up here and they’ll be in touch. “Readers overseas: send us a message or request a quote at the same link to register interest. If we hear from enough people in one area, we can bring forward our plans to come there.”

Having proven their point, Thermal Dawn is cleared to sell and installing its first batch now, with a larger product for ducted air conditioning in development. I asked about apartment block heating and Nick confirmed that they are looking at it but want to get the domestic home sorted first.

I asked a couple of followup questions “What about the Victorian government’s position?” Nick’s answer:  “Victoria is set to bring in support for systems like ours from the middle of next year. With the state election in November, there’s talk of a change in direction and of belt-tightening, so we’ve built Thermal Dawn to stand on its own. It saves households money without a subsidy, and any support is a bonus.”

Any plans for installs in Canberra? “Yes. Canberra is one of the best places in Australia for this: cold winters, plenty of hydronic homes, and a territory already moving off gas. We’re talking with installers there now.”

I really appreciate these technological experts when they take the time to explain things to me. Sometimes I feel like Winnie the Pooh — a bear of very little brain. Looks like Thermal Dawn has solved another part of the energy puzzle — good news for homeowners and also for the planet.

David Waterworth is a retired teacher who divides his time between looking after his grandchildren and trying to make sure they have a planet to live on. He is long on Tesla [NASDAQ:TSLA].

#5864. 1968 Ford Mustang For Sale Is A Clean, Green V8 Cruiser Begging To Be Driven Daily

When you hear "green 1968 Ford Mustang," you likely picture one very specific car. You know the one: a verdant, tire-killing fastback driven by mercurial automotive and Hollywood legend Steve McQueen in the 1968 film "Bullitt." Today, a first-generation Ford Mustang Fastback similar to the one from the 58-year-old action-crime thriller could demand six figures, especially in that oh-so coveted color: Highland Green. For first-gen Mustang fans who can't afford to spend fixer-upper-home money on a car, there are alternatives. Alternatives like this green 1968 Ford Mustang.

At a glance and on paper, it ticks boxes. A V8 under the hood? Of course. That classic facelifted first-generation Mustang look? Thankfully, it's intact. Mostly. See, someone thought this one was deserving of a cool restomod treatment, and it got just that. Instead of being a numbers-matching carbureted survivor, this one benefits from a myriad of modern and aftermarket updates, like electronic fuel injection, electric fans, power locks, keyless entry, and Vintage Air air-conditioning and heat. This is a daily-driver-ready take on a classic. It's up for grabs, too. As of this writing, the restomod-ed Mustang is for sale just north of Dallas. Purists need not apply.

No, it's not finished in Highland Green. Not even close, really. The 1968 Ford Mustang restomod currently for sale by PC Classic Cars in Sherman, Texas is a much lighter hue. The headlights have been replaced with an integrated LED lamp-and-signal set and the tail lights are sequential like an aftermarket set you'd find on a much newer Mustang. It also rides on a set of staggered two-tone Halibrand-style alloy wheels that complement the paintwork, wrapped up in Nitto rubber. The builder also swapped in a Mustang II front end, complete with a sway bar and tubular control arms.

Under the hood, the '68 Mustang gets a familiar engine option: a 289-cubic-inch V8. It's far from stock, though. The parts list continues with a set of aluminum AFR cylinder heads, a Holley Sniper EFI setup, a Fi-Tech electronic ignition, an aftermarket serpentine system, an aluminum radiator in place of the tired old stock unit, and dual electric fans, to name a few things. The whole thing hooks up to a four-speed automatic gearbox with overdrive. Sorry, no manual here.

There are more modern touches beyond the engine bay, including power locks with keyless entry via an aftermarket fob, a stereo system with an amplifier and subwoofers, and that Vintage Air climate control. The restomod treatment continues inside the classic Mustang's cabin. It's a full brown leather TMI interior with black accents on the folding bucket seats and dash paneling. The brown leather even extends into the trunk.

It's not perfect. A glance at the driver's side door reveals a little misalignment. The car was once red. There are blemishes here and there. In short, this is more of a driver, less of a concours condition car meant to be kept out of the rain or prolonged direct sunlight. That doesn't mean the modified pony car loses the aesthetic charm that landed the 1968 model on the list of your favorite Ford Mustangs. Well, the fastback did, at least.

So just how much does PC Classic Cars want for this one? It's currently on sale for $46,950. That's quite a bit steeper than the average $25,310 price of 1968 Ford Mustang coupé sales over the last year. Then again, not every '68 Mustang on the market has had this much work done.

Get this: Its clock shows just 119 miles. Though, as you might expect, that's not exactly accurate. It's likely that this build's underpinnings have a much higher mileage. Frankly, a 1968 Ford Mustang with a 289-cubic-inch V8 and an true odometer reading anywhere near 119 would demand a much, much higher price. Still, with the modern tweaks already on this 58-year-old 'Stang, it seriously needs a driver to take it on as a daily and run that odometer up. After all, what would McQueen do? He'd almost certainly drive it — and so should the next owner.

#5863. Ayrton Senna's Honda NSX Sells For Record $1.1 Million At Auction

One of the original NSX's biggest selling points was that Honda recruited three-time Formula 1 champion Ayrton Senna to help develop the sports car. While the legendary Brazilian wasn't impressed with the NSX at first, it evolved into a mass-produced machine he eventually praised. Senna's personal 1991 Honda NSX sold for $1.17 million at RM Sotheby's auction in London last week. The sale made the late champion's car the most expensive first-generation NSX ever sold at auction, surpassing a $1.06 million mark set for a 2003 NSX-R last year.

Honda was contractually obligated to provide Senna with an NSX for his personal use. The Japanese automaker supplied three examples of the sports car, a pair in black and one in Formula Red. The red NSX, the auctioned car, was stored in Portugal and delivered to Senna when he visited the country. It's the same car that the Brazilian was photographed washing with a garden hose. The 1992 documentary "Ayrton Senna: Racing Is In My Blood" also features Senna spinning the wheels on this NSX. After Senna's death in 1994, the sports car stayed with the Portuguese dealership that owned it until 1997.

Senna's most successful period in F1 came with McLaren from 1988 until 1993. The Brazilian won three F1 world championships and 35 races over the six seasons with the British team. Honda supplied engines to McLaren, ending the partnership after the 1992 season. If by fate, McLaren conducted a preseason test at Suzuka Circuit in February 1989, just as Honda's R&D department was wrapping up its month-long NSX testing program. The engineers let Senna run laps in the sports car. According to Road & Track, Senna wasn't pleased, stating, "I'm not sure I can really give you appropriate advice on a mass-production car, but I feel it's a little fragile."

Honda went back to the drawing board and increased the NSX's chassis stiffness by 50%. The automaker even invited Senna back to test the sports car at the Nürburgring and help tune the suspension. The expert input played a significant role in the NSX's success, from marketing to the sports car's critical success. While most of us didn't have the budget to bid on Senna's NSX, Honda is doing its part to help other NSX owners keep their cars just as pristine. The Japanese automaker's heritage program now produces over 3,000 official reproduction parts to keep first-generation NSXs on the road and running smoothly.

#5862. 'Forever Chemicals' Linked to Aggressive Breast Cancers

— Findings have "important public health implications," researchers say

Two common "forever chemicals" were associated with a higher risk of estrogen receptor (ER)-negative breast cancer, a prospective case-cohort study suggested.

The highest exposure quartile of perfluoro-n-octanoic acid (PFOA) was associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer compared with the lowest quartile (HR 1.67, 95% CI 1.10-2.53), and the same was true for perfluorooctane-1-sulfonic acid (PFOS; HR 1.93, 95% CI 1.15-3.22), reported Alexandra J. White, PhD, of the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, and colleagues.

A meta-analysis of seven studies further supported an association for PFOA (relative risk [RR] 1.30, 95% CI 1.05-1.62), and less so for PFOS (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.91-1.58), they noted in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

"Our positive findings were generally concentrated among hormone receptor-negative tumors," White and team wrote, adding that this suggests that per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) "may act through nonhormonal mechanisms, consistent with the evidence that many PFAS are only weak endocrine disrupting chemicals and that other relevant mechanisms, such as epigenetic alterations and immunosuppression, may underlie these associations."

"These findings have important public health implications given the limited established risk factors for ER-negative tumors, which are generally more aggressive," they concluded.

White told MedPage Today that "there are a lot of factors related to a woman's risk of developing breast cancer. Our findings suggest these chemicals may be one contributor to ER-negative breast cancer risk specifically, and if women have concerns about their PFAS exposure, reducing exposure to sources such as contaminated water would be a very reasonable step."

She pointed out that the compounds assessed here "have been phased out from industry and largely replaced by other PFAS compounds. Most of us still have measurable levels of these compounds in our bodies and it is important to document the different health outcomes or cancer tumor sites that are related to exposure to these compounds."

"From a public health perspective, we probably want to start shifting our focus to the health effects of these replacement PFAS compounds that are being used more today," she added.

There have been several other studies that have demonstrated positive associations between PFOS and PFOA and ER-negative tumors, including an analysis of the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial and a French study.

For this analysis, the authors used the Sister Study, a prospective cohort of 50,884 breast cancer-free women ages 35 to 74, each of whom had a full or half-sister diagnosed with breast cancer, enrolled in the U.S. and Puerto Rico between 2003 and 2009.

The researchers included 1,609 women who developed breast cancer and a comparison sample of 2,269 women. They were followed for a median of 5.9 and 9.7 years, and had a median baseline age of 57.2 and 55.6 years, respectively.

White observed that she and her team oversampled women with ER-negative tumors to improve the study's statistical power. "These tumors are less frequently diagnosed and so they've been harder to study," she said.

White and her team quantified 17 PFAS in prediagnostic plasma using liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry.

They also observed a potential link between n-methylperfluoro-1-octanesulfonamidoacetic acid and ER-negative breast cancer, although that association did not reach statistical significance (HR 1.42, 95% CI 0.99-2.04).

On the other hand, perfluoro-n-tridecanoic acid was inversely associated with ER-negative tumors (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.41-0.97).

Perfluorooctane sulfonamide (PFOSA), which was not commonly detected (6.9%), was positively associated with ER-positive tumors (HR 1.36, 95% CI 1.03-1.81).

Regarding overall breast cancer incidence, White and colleagues found that PFOSA showed a trend toward higher risk among patients with detectable versus non-detectable concentrations (HR 1.29, 95% CI 0.99-1.67), while perfluoro-n-decanoic acid showed a "suggestive" positive association (HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.95-1.44).

There were "negligible" associations between the rest of the PFAS and overall breast cancer incidence.

#5861. How Can Europe Accelerate Electric Trucking?

Europe is having a hard time lately, with skyrocketing oil prices dampening economies. Fuel costs, particularly diesel, are prompting surging interest in truck electrification. Europe has been urging truck makers to move toward electric trucking, and they have responded with a variety of electric semi trucks from many manufacturers. Europe is a group of sovereign countries with many standards. The European Union is a political and economic union of 27 states in that area. It issued directives urging action and imposing penalties. In response to European Union directives, companies have formed EV100, a coalition of corporations responding to the need. In a recent story, Steve Hanley wrote about European electric truck makers’ difficulties expanding truck electrification. Here’s a quotation from the story: “In a letter to EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, of primary concern, in their estimation, is expanding the charging infrastructure for heavy-duty trucks in Europe.” There is no shortage of electric trucks in Europe. Expansion could go faster were it not for charging infrastructure. Manufacturers complain about “an alarming delay” in conditions needed to drive market uptake. For Europe, truck electrification is not working as well as in China, where over 90% of the world’s electric trucks reside. The differences between China and the EU show some reasons why truck electrification is slower in Europe. How did China succeed where the EU failed? China made electric trucks a freight system, not a vehicle category.

Power is a major factor in electric grid infrastructure. Charging electric trucks places demands on power. Peak power determines how much infrastructure is necessary. In grid planning, peak annual power determines how much capital equipment is necessary. Reducing peak power demand is a critical factor for electric truck infrastructure. Figure 1 shows one method of reducing power called route stuffing. It schedules departures on heavy traffic corridors at regularly spaced intervals. Corridors like ones between ports and warehouses are a target for those practices. These corridors often route trucks in a round trip chain. Filling routes with scheduled trips can reduce power demand compared to random trip scheduling. The article Battery Swap Uses Fewer Batteries Than You Think is devoted to methods of analysis and planning that can lead to lower peak power demand. There are other benefits to planning, such as greater truck load capacity from the same amount of batteries. Part of the solution to slow electric truck infrastructure development is to plan infrastructure and truck use practices to reduce the charging power burden. Given the pressing and enduring need due to the diesel fuel cost crisis, it is necessary to reprioritize grid power upgrade demands. Demands for data center power upgrades like transformers for substations should be re shuffled and prioritized toward the diesel crisis.

In two articles, Michael Barnard outlined the issues. Vehicles are not a transportation system. What does Europe have now? It has an EU Commission interacting with a coalition, EV100. The problem is, there are plenty of trucks available, but who is in charge of infrastructure? You can’t have electric trucks without means of charging, but as the coalition complains, “Significant improvements to charging infrastructure, a reduction in carbon dioxide based tolls, and a coherent policy framework are urgently needed.” There are so many stakeholders — including the commission, vehicles makers, and charging companies across multiple countries — that no one is in charge of infrastructure, and without it, nothing moves. It needs a unity of purpose and action.

If China is succeeding, why not adopt its strategy? Perhaps the answer is right in front of everyone’s nose. As Michael puts it, “the policy connects vehicles to corridors, depots, service areas, grids and freight use cases instead of treating sales targets as sufficient.” CATL offered Europe a system, not a vehicle. This is a “turn key” solution. It’s a well thought out system, including use of methods and practices, not an anything goes free-for-all. That kind of stability and predictability is what EV100 leaders are looking for. This is not a swap-or-nothing scenario. Different techniques apply to various use cases. Swap must be planned for high-use freight corridors and other proper applications. Swap trucks can also fast charge or slow charge, providing flexibility and a system of trucks that includes smaller trucks, not just semis.

What does all this have to do with Europe’s slowly advancing infrastructure? Simply put, electric trucks put heavy charging demands on the grid. Trucks can have megawatt-hour batteries that require megawatt power charging to charge in an hour. Reducing grid power demands can reduce grid infrastructure upgrade costs, and leverage capital investment toward faster implementation.

“The process of getting megawatt charging equipment connected to the grid can take several years, delaying deployment even where operators and infrastructure providers are ready to invest.” The need for megawatt charging equipment is reduced by accelerating swap network development instead of fixed battery trucks that must be charged by fast chargers. “Swaptopus is easy to misread as a quirky name for another electric-truck infrastructure project. It is a newly formed joint venture between Octopus Energy and CATL, created to develop automated battery-swapping hubs for heavy trucks across Europe.” Unlike the government of China that played a role in encouraging standards and cooperation in infrastructure, Europe has a looser arrangement between many countries with various standards. Europe is learning the slow, hard way where battery swapping is most needed.

Every truck application has different optimization. It means that there must be different approaches to fit freight operations in heavy traffic corridors. Quoting Michael Barnard, “Freight operators often run repeated routes between ports, factories, distribution centres and logistics hubs. Those patterns provide known traffic, known stopping points and relatively predictable electricity demand. A swap hub can be placed around an existing freight flow instead of hoping that enough unrelated trucks eventually pass through.”

Freight corridors are a scenario made to order for battery swap. Real trucking solutions include a mix of vehicle and infrastructure types — from small, local delivery, to large, long-haul freight; and from slow, overnight charging, to medium power charging and battery swap — all used in concert to accelerate heavy truck electrification. With a wide variety of charging options, and vehicles and charging use cases targeted in coordination to avoid peak power demands, the path forward is eased. School buses don’t need expensive high-power fast charging. Lower-power chargers can do the trick. Local delivery can use a mix of overnight and medium power charging. Heavy truck dispatch must be more carefully coordinated to avoid peak demand and grid upgrade costs. A mix of medium-power charging and swap stations along with planned use cases can successfully lower electric freight power needs and transport system capital expenses to speed transport electrification.

Transformation and conversion of diesel freight systems to electric requires coordination and planning between government agencies and coalitions of corporations, cities, government agencies, and planners. Grid expansion and construction can take years. #5860. U.S. Acura Dealers Are Now Selling 3,000 Factory Reproduction Parts For Your OG NSX

News about Honda making and selling new reproduction parts for the first-generation NSX has been brewing for more than a year now, but it's finally, actually here. The Honda Heritage Parts program launched in Japan back in April but is now making its way stateside. The automaker announced Monday that more than 3,000 Genuine Honda Reproduction Parts for its first-ever supercar are now available for purchase at Acura dealerships across the U.S. and via the online Honda DreamShop. There are apparently plans for "future expansion" of the program, as well.

The American Honda Motor Co. hasn't released a master list of all 3,000 parts being offered, but taking a quick gander at the program's Japanese webpage shows a wide range of stuff available. You can get a camshaft for the yen equivalent of about $850, an accelerator pedal assembly costs $340, and the car's entire V6 cylinder block can be had for around $6,300. If you're a fan looking for some merch-type items, a little armrest emblem that says "NSX DOHC VTEC" on it and the Japanese NSX owner's manual go for about $40 and $60, respectively.

The O.G. NSX (known to Honda nerds as the NA1 and NA2) was branded in America as an Acura and was sold from model years 1991 to 2005, and the newly produced parts apply to NSXs across that entire production run. The program is called Honda Heritage Parts, by the way, not Honda NSX Heritage Parts, which means reproduced parts for other classic Hondas are almost certainly coming in the future.

From Acura's press release: "Honda Heritage Parts was created to help our customers enjoy their classic Acura and Honda performance models, and it's appropriate that we begin with an iconic model like the first-generation Acura NSX," said American Honda executive vice president Mamadou Diallo (though the emphasis is mine). As the owner of a 2004 S2000 that could definitely use some rejuvenation here and there, hopefully that's the next Honda to get the Heritage Parts treatment.

#5859. Trump Is Gonna Cave On Offshore Wind In 5…4…3…

…JK! US President Donald Trump will never cry surrender in the war against offshore wind turbines. The President was burned once before, when a wind farm arose in Aberdeen Bay in Scotland, within view of a Trump-branded golf course back in the early 2000’s. Never again! The President has taken extreme measures to prevent such blight from tainting the shores of the United States. Nevertheless, scores of the pesky oversized pinwheels have already eluded the Trump chopper, and many more are on the way.

The latest news concerns CVOW, the 2.6-gigwatt Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project under the wing of the leading utility Dominion. As the name of the project indicates, CVOW sits in the Atlantic Ocean about 24 nautical miles (28 land miles) off the coast of Virginia Beach, Virginia.

CVOW began taking shape during Trump’s first turn around the Oval Office, and construction was well under way when his second term began on January 20, 2025.

Immediately upon taking office, Trump abruptly suspended the offshore wind lease program administered by the Department of the Interior. He also ordered spurious re-reviews of offshore projects that were already in the permitting pipeline, and he had the Department of Justice administer a legally questionable buy-back program to prevent activity from stirring among other lease holders. In addition, he had the Interior Department issue multiple emergency orders aimed at stopping five offshore projects off the coasts of Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, Maryland, and Massachusetts, where construction work was already well under way.

So far, though, only one part of the effort has stuck. Last year a federal judge affirmed that any President, Trump or not, has the authority to stop issuing new offshore leases. However, the same judge decided there is no blanket authority to suspend offshore leases that are already in the permitting process. The buy-back program is also in litigation, with critics raising questions about the funds used to pay off lease holders among other issues.

Additionally,  the Interior Department failed to convince multiple federal judges that the emergency orders had any merit. Work has continued on all five Atlantic coast projects, including CVOW.

CVOW began delivering its first kilowatts to shore in March, and Dominion recapped its progress on the wind farm in its Q3 report on October 30. As handily summarized by the news organization Maritime Executive, the project currently clocks in at 85% complete. All of the main turbine components — nacelles, towers, and blades — for the wind farm’s 176 offshore wind turbines have been fabricated. Forty-four have been fully installed so far. With a 45th coming any day now, the wind farm currently hosts 640 megawatts out of the 2,600 megawatt total.

Since Trump declared an “Energy Emergency” in January of 2025, it’s fair to ask why he has spent so much time, energy and taxpayer dollars to crush an entire domestic energy industry. After all, if one was not reading too closely between the lines of the declaration, the new energy policy is little more than a rehash of former President Barack Obama’s “All Of The Above” energy policy. As further embellished by Energy Secretary Chris Wright, the new version specifically taps multiple zero and low-emission energy resources for support including nuclear energy, biomass, hydropower, and geothermal energy, just like Obama did, along the emerging field of marine energy, which was barely a speck on the horizon while Obama was in office.

Energy storage, and the critical minerals needed in the clean tech industry, have also been gathered up in a Trumpian embrace.

Conspicuously absent, however, are the two most abundant, economical, and easily accessible domestic energy resources, namely, wind and solar.

If there really was an energy emergency…oh, never mind! Despite Trump’s complaints, offshore wind is a mature industry with a vigorous supply global supply chain and support equipment, as deftly illustrated by the CVOW project. In the October 30 report, Dominion noted that it takes only about two days for an offshore construction vessel to install a wind turbine on its foundation.

While the offshore wind construction timetable is subject to weather delays, Dominion also stated that the project is on schedule — despite any further delays related to last year’s stop-work order.

Speaking of the stop-work order, CVOW was conspicuously excluded from previous rounds of stop-work orders impacting the four other Atlantic coast wind farms under construction in 2025. If you’re guessing that Virginia’s Republican Governor, Glenn Youngkin, had a hand in that decision, drop a note in the discussion thread. Youngkin publicly supported the CVOW project but he was term-limited out of office last year. A stop-work order would have put an embarrassing crimp in his next-step political plans. The order came down only after Election Day 2025, after the Democratic candidate, Abigail Spanberger, won the post.

In a classic case of karma biting back, CVOW is a  more efficient and economical project than initially envisioned. A round of delays during Trump’s first term in office gave Dominion an opportunity to redesign the project with next-generation wind turbines. Those delays also enabled Dominion to take advantage of a new generation of turbine installation vessels that are purpose-built to cut offshore construction costs.

The results speak for themselves. In its October 30 report, Dominion indicated that CVOW costs were still consistent with its capital budget, even accounting for the cost of last year’s stop-work order and costs related to Trump’s tariff wars.

“The estimates on the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) also continue to fall,” Maritime Executive summarized. “After starting with a forecasted range of $80-$90 per MWh, and adjustments for changes after the change in administrations, they have lowered the LCOE to $62, down from an estimate of $83 presented in August” (LCOE is a calculation that provides a common ground for comparing costs among different forms of power generation).

Maritime Executive further reported that Dominion expects to save its ratepayers about $5 billion on fuel over the first 10 years of operation.

Trump’s war on wind has also petered out elsewhere. The Revolution Wind project off the coasts of Connecticut and Massachusetts has also been a target of  multiple stop-work orders over the past two years, with the latest hammer coming down just two weeks ago, when the 704-megawatt wind farm was almost complete.

Revolution Wind is now fully operational, joining the nearby Vineyard Wind project which also endured multiple attacks from Trump. As reported by public radio station WBUR, the savings from Revolution Wind is expected to ripple out through New England, saving $500 million for ratepayers in the region every year.

As for the domestic offshore wind industry writ large, the US lost thousands of onshore supply chain jobs all around the US in addition to job losses related to portside and offshore operation. However, the trade organization Oceantic Network is already prepping for a comeback. “The road to recovery for the embattled American offshore wind industry starts today with a new political mandate to tackle the affordability crisis,” Oceantic President and CEO Liz said in a public statement celebrating the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in the 202y midterm elections.

Suzuki has long been, for better and for worse, a motorcycle maker that keeps its old assembly lines running. While the company comes up with something truly new every once in a while, it's more likely to figure out a new combination of parts it already has laying around. So, for EICMA, we shouldn't be surprised that Suzuki's big announcements are based around engines old enough to drink. We also shouldn't be surprised that those engines are inside what look to be some damn good bikes.

Suzuki's big reveals this year are the SV-7S and GSX-10R, bikes built around the 27-year-old SV650 engine and 21-year-old K5 GSX-R1000 engines, respectively. The former looks to be a mild update to the outgoing SV650, with new lighting, emissions equipment, a quickshifter, and a ride-by-wire throttle wrapped around the prior bike's frame and engine. Most importantly, the SV-7S is available in Europe, meaning that the 645 cc V-twin lives on under Euro 5+ emissions. Suzuki's site doesn't list power claims for the new bike, but it's likely to make the same 73 horses it has since time immemorial.

While the SV-7S is an update and a name change for the SV650, the GSX-10R (above) is ostensibly an entirely new bike — admittedly a bike that's largely just a faired version of the GSX-S1000, the company's naked literbike. Despite the similar displacement, the GSX-10R is nothing like the top-tier GSX-R1000. Instead, it's closer to a revival of the beloved K5 GSX-R1000 of the mid-aughts.

Yet, no matter what Reddit says, the GSX-10R is more than just a reheated leftover K5. Its name points to the difference, putting the bike in line with the GSX-8R — Suzuki intends the new 10R to be more streetable than the highest-test Gixxer, with lower footpegs, USB power, and a torque-rich engine for those times you can't sit at redline. There's also a full suite of electronics, to assist everything from traction to braking, launches, engine braking, hill starts, and cruising.

If the GSX-10R turns out to be what Suzuki says — a four-cylinder GSX-8R, a literbike with K5 reliability and daily-rider comfort — it could be the EICMA release I'm most excited to swing a leg over. To know for sure, though, I'll have to figure out how to get my hands on one.

#5857. Infant Bleeding Rises as Newborn Vitamin K Shots Have Fallen

— Brain bleed risk more than doubled in infants who missed routine vitamin K shots

Newborns who missed routine vitamin K shots had higher bleeding risks and more than double the risk of intracranial hemorrhage, a nationwide study of over 5 million infants showed.

Infants who did not receive prophylactic vitamin K shots, the share of which increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, had a 47% higher bleeding risk by 6 months (288.0 vs 185.9 per 10,000; adjusted risk ratio [RR] 1.47, 95% CI 1.43-1.51), reported Heather Burris, MD, MPH, of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, and colleagues in JAMA.

They also had more than twice the risks of intracranial bleeding (33.0 vs 13.2 per 10,000; adjusted RR 2.43, 95% CI 2.26-2.62) and death with concurrent bleeding during the birth hospitalization (2.9 vs 1.1 per 10,000; adjusted RR 2.69, 95% CI 2.09-3.47).

Diagnosed vitamin K deficiency tripled in infants and vitamin K deficiency bleeding more than quadrupled during this period, noted Elizabeth Wolf, MD, MPH, of Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond, and co-authors in a related JAMA Pediatrics research letter.

Among children ages 0 to 6 months, the rate of vitamin K deficiency climbed from 11.8 to 37.3 per 100,000 from 2017 to 2025, while vitamin K deficiency bleeding rose from 24.0 to 107.4 per 100,000.

Brain hemorrhages occurred in 6.9% of infants diagnosed with vitamin K deficiency and 2.4% of those with vitamin K-deficient bleeding.

Both studies leveraged electronic health record data from January 2017 through December 2025 using the Epic Cosmos research platform to evaluate infants born at 35 weeks' gestation or later. The JAMA study followed 5.24 million newborns for the first 6 months of life. The JAMA Pediatrics study evaluated 11 million U.S. infants ages 0 to 6 months who received care from 2017 through 2025.

Vitamin K is required to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, Wolf and co-authors noted. Newborns can be deficient in vitamin K due to low transplacental transfer, limited gut synthesis, low breast milk concentration, and poor gastrointestinal absorption, they said.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended vitamin K shots since 1961. However, parental rejection of prophylactic vitamin K has increased in recent years, placing more infants at risk for vitamin K deficiency bleeding, Wolf and colleagues observed.

"This study shows the real-world consequences of vitamin K refusal," Wolf told MedPage Today. "Vitamin K-deficient bleeding can be very serious in babies. When the bleeding occurs in the brain, it can result in permanent neurologic damage or even death."

Classical vitamin K deficiency occurs between 2 days and 1 week after birth and leads to umbilical bleeding and bruising. Late vitamin K deficiency occurs between ages 1 week and 6 months and has a 30% to 60% risk of intracranial hemorrhage. Studies have shown that infants without vitamin K shots were 81 times more likely to develop late vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

Temporal trends in the JAMA study showed year-over-year increases in the number of infants with bleeding and these trends differed significantly by vitamin K receipt, noted Laura Kair, MD, MAS, of the University of California Davis School of Medicine in Sacramento, and colleagues in an accompanying editorial.

"While the causes underlying these trends remain uncertain, the authors speculate that maternal-infant dyads may have had more severe medical comorbidities in recent years, and they emphasize that bleeding rates rose significantly faster among those with vitamin K nonreceipt," Kair and colleagues wrote.

"As with all serious but rare outcomes, vitamin K deficiency bleeding risk is a difficult concept to communicate, and when presented as a percentage may seem purely theoretical," the editorialists noted.

"Based on the authors' calculation of number needed to harm, one additional infant would have a bleeding event if just 114 infants did not receive vitamin K," Kair and co-authors pointed out. "This number needed to harm provides a powerful narrative that may be more readily accessible to parents, supporting more effective counseling and decision-making."

Study limitations included reliance on Epic Cosmos data, which excludes infants treated at facilities using other electronic health record systems.

"In countries such as France, Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Canada, oral vitamin K is offered either routinely or alternatively to intramuscular vitamin K," wrote Wolf and colleagues. "Although the oral form can be less effective in preventing late vitamin K deficiency, a harm-reduction approach that offers oral vitamin K as a second-line alternative may be warranted in the U.S. if rejection of injectable vitamin K continues."

#5854. America’s New Shipbuilding Orders Are Expensive Bets on Fossil Freight

South Korea’s Hanwha Group owns the Philadelphia shipyard that has become a centerpiece of Washington’s attempt to rebuild American commercial shipbuilding. Its Hanwha Ocean and Hanwha Systems subsidiaries acquired the US yard in December 2024. The investment creates and sustains American production capacity and jobs while transferring shipbuilding expertise, technology and training from South Korea to US workers. The facility is in America, but its corporate ownership remains South Korean. The company’s published orderbook, however, tells a more complicated story: two liquefied natural gas carriers, four firm orders for oil and chemical tankers, and options for another six tankers. Three LNG-fueled container ships ordered by Matson in 2022 predate the current administration. The newer LNG and tanker orders come from Hanwha’s own shipping affiliates. They can help restart production, but buying ships from another company in the same group does not demonstrate that independent shipowners will pay US construction prices.

The price gap is difficult to dismiss. Kinder Morgan’s January 2026 investor presentation estimates that a new medium-range Jones Act tanker would cost more than $240 million and require a long-term charter above $115,000 per day to justify construction. The existing charter market was around $90,000 per day. Kinder Morgan operates 16 tankers, with its fleet fully utilized, yet the gap between current charter revenue and the cost of a replacement vessel remains substantial. High utilization establishes a need for shipping services; it does not establish a financeable order for a new American-built tanker at today’s prices.

Coastal petroleum shipping also competes with other domestic infrastructure. A 2025 report to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission estimated moving gasoline from Houston to New York Harbor at under 8 cents per gallon by pipeline, about 20 cents by ship, and roughly 35 cents by rail. These illustrative route costs do not cover every destination, and tankers remain essential where pipelines are unavailable. They do show why expensive new tankers cannot count on charter customers accepting whatever price domestic construction requires. Longer term, the International Energy Agency estimates that electric vehicles displaced 1.7 million barrels of oil per day worldwide in 2025 and could displace about 5 million by 2030 under its policy scenarios. That does not mean US tanker demand vanishes, but fleet investment must account for changes in the cargo market over several decades.

LNG export carriers have a more plausible near-term growth market, although their prospects are different from the prospects of LNG-fueled container ships. US gas exports may expand, and LNG tankers will be needed to carry them. The commercial test for a US-built LNG carrier is whether it can win an arm’s-length contract against established Korean, Japanese and Chinese shipyards. Hanwha’s plan to train Philadelphia workers through its Korean shipyards can strengthen US industrial capability, and affiliated orders can provide an initial production run. The central uncertainty is whether independent buyers will still choose these ships once the group’s internal demand and any cargo preference are removed.

A broader domestic vessel market already exists. US-flag Great Lakes freighters carried 71.3 million tons in 2025, much of it iron ore, limestone, cement, coal and other bulk materials. Those cargo flows will change as steelmaking and energy systems evolve, while ferry services, harbour vessels, inland cargo craft and multipurpose ships will still require renewal. Battery-electric and hybrid-electric propulsion offer practical options on routes with manageable energy requirements and reliable charging access. Large, long-distance bulk ships need a more selective technology assessment, rather than an assumption that every vessel can run on batteries.

Recent projects demonstrate what a committed customer can contribute to ship economics. CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept launched an electric inland barge in Vietnam for a 180-kilometre round trip. Nike agreed to fill 90% of its capacity for eight years, helping justify a vessel reportedly costing about twice as much as its diesel equivalent. A dedicated charging installation and renewable electricity form part of the service. That is a commercially structured freight proposition, with its higher capital cost supported by contracted utilization and expected operating savings.

Electric propulsion does not cure the American shipbuilding cost problem by itself. Washington State’s three new hybrid-electric ferries carry a $714.5 million shipbuilding contract, and the state’s estimate including additional equipment and other program expenses is approximately $1.15 billion. Construction has started; the ferries are not yet in service. The path to a productive shipbuilding industry still runs through standardized designs, modular fabrication, trained workers, repeat orders, reliable delivery and falling labor-hours per vessel. It would be a mistake to treat electrification as a substitute for manufacturing reform.

Hanwha’s South Korean capital and know-how could contribute to that reform by developing US suppliers and production skills that serve several vessel classes. That is a meaningful way to rebuild domestic capability even though the parent company remains foreign-owned. Its progress should ultimately be measured by independent repeat customers, improving construction costs and commercially competitive vessels, rather than affiliated orders or investment announcements. A US maritime strategy anchored to the fossil-fuel cargoes of today risks missing a growing opportunity to build modern domestic vessels for the freight, port and ferry services of tomorrow.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Hanwha’s orders, Kinder Morgan’s tanker economics and the market for repeatable electric and hybrid maritime construction. It follows my earlier analysis of the Jones Act’s shipbuilding capacity gap.

#5853. At $18,900, Is This Incredibly Low-Mileage 1986 Chrysler LeBaron Town & Country A Woody You Would Buy?

With just 3,800 miles on the clock, today's Nice Price or No Dice LeBaron Town & Country is a true time capsule of '80s glory. It even has a bench seat in the front! Now priced about 30% more than when it was new, we'll have to decide whether it's worth it to feel the MTV-era vibes.

With the introduction of the Prius in the late 1990s, Toyota rewrote the meaning of a "hybrid auto." Before the Prius mated electric and internal combustion motors for power, a hybrid auto typically meant an American engine in a European car. The Sunbeam Tiger with its British-built body and Ford 289 was a hybrid. So too were the Iso Rivolta and the clutch of Bizzarrini, which sported Chevy small-block power.

The 2013 Cadillac Escalade we looked at on Thursday is a hybrid in the modern sense, featuring a gearbox employing two electric motors to aid the V8 engine in both driving the SUV and keeping its high-voltage battery full of electrons. That was, and still is, a fiddly system with a number of known failure points. On top of that, our Escalade already had 140K under its belt, so those failures could be expected at any given time. Those factors led to warnings in the comments and eventually, a 65% 'No Dice' loss for the Caddy's $11,995 asking price.

In the 1933 novel "Lost Horizon" by James Hilton, a small group of Westerners survives a plane crash high in a remote, uncharted part of the Himalayas. There, they discover a lamasery—Shangri-La—which seemingly has magical properties that slow aging among its inhabitants. This comes at a high cost: the inhabitants are trapped there, because leaving means rapidly aging and dying. I know, bummer.

Today's 1986 Chrysler LeBaron Town & Country looks like it was just magically freed from some mystical Shangri-La, as it appears in as-new, almost entirely original condition and has less than 4,000 miles on the clock. How did this come to be? The seller has a succinct recap in the ad:

Back in 1986 a man bought his wife the finest station wagon Chrysler produced, this LeBaron Town & Country TURBO wagon. She only drove it 1500 miles before parking it in the garage when she became ill, and ultimately passed. The car ended up in climate controlled storage at a Chrysler dealer for 30 years. Then during Covid it was brought back to life with a new gas tank, driven a couple hundred miles and ended up on consignment at World Wide Autos in Colorado.

The current owner bought the car four years ago, brought it to Georgia, and replaced all the rubber bits, fluids, and the non-working factory stereo. Other than those updates, this K Car is claimed to be just as it left the factory.

This Town & Country has the goods, too. An unexpected decal on the hood announces the engine: a 2.2-liter Chrysler four with fuel injection and a Garrett T03 turbocharger. The motor was factory-rated at 146 horsepower and 168 pound-feet of torque, which might not seem like all that and a bag of chips today, but back in the mid-'80s it was pretty impressive.

Befitting this car's role as a Town & Country cruiser, the motor is mated to a three-speed TorqueFlite automatic which drives the front wheels.

According to the ad, the car is 100% roadworthy and even has working R12 A/C. Before the current owner took possession, a previous owner replaced the gas tank. That, the rubber, and the radio are apparently the only hard bits of the car that aren't factory original. That makes this LeBaron a total time capsule, and the seller boasts it's a hit at many local car shows.

Of course, this also has the look that anyone with an "I HEART THE '80s" tattoo will simply gush over. There's an old joke about a traveler stopping into a bar in the South and asking what kind of music they play there, to which the bartender replies, "Oh, we got both types: country AND western." This LeBaron is similarly a Town & Country model, meaning it has the faux woodgrain paneling down its flanks emulating the classic Town & Country Chryslers of the 1940s. That's in amazing condition with no apparent fading or damage. Under that is a coat of elegant black paint that looks to be simple, single-stage. Chrome wire wheel covers complete the picture.

There's more old-school goodness in the cabin, as it features a wide split-bench seat in the front, clean gray cloth upholstery, and a low center tunnel afforded by the FWD layout that offers a ton of foot room.

This is a high-end K-car, so it has power windows and locks, cruise control, a tilt wheel, and the aforementioned A/C. The modern Sony stereo is a bit of a letdown, but is probably more useful than the non-working original, even if it spoils the overall throwback experience.

This LeBaron comes with a clean title, and the seller suggests that while museums are welcome to snap it up, the wagon should really be enjoyed on the road. That, of course, means adding to its miles, which takes away one of the car's unique ownership aspects. Maybe put it on a flatbed and drive it around so you can enjoy the experience without ruining that uber-low mileage fame.

Whatever the choice, we'll now have to consider LeBaron's $18,900 asking price. That's a good bit higher than the around $12K it cost when new, but inflation has taken its toll, and honestly, where are you going to find another one in this condition and spec? Supply and demand is one of the first things they teach you in Econ 101.

What do you think about this LeBaron and that $18,900 asking? Do you feel like a buyer should be resigned to pay that price given the car's rarity and condition? Or is that too much even if this LeBaron offers both Town AND Country?

#5852. DUOTAP Trial: Postdilation Sets Up TAVR for Success

— Extra step optimizes transcatheter heart valve geometry for better downstream hemodynamics

Routine postdilation conferred several upsides in transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a balloon-expandable platform, according to emerging trial evidence.

In the DUOTAP trial, routine postdilation largely corrected any Sapien device asymmetry, with transcatheter heart valve (THV) asymmetry index on fluoroscopy reduced by 70% compared to TAVR without postdilation, in the optimization of THV geometry, according to Maximilian Autherith, MD, of the Medical University of Vienna.

This was associated with downstream benefits, such as a 67% reduction in more-than-mild paravalvular leak (PVL) on pre-discharge echocardiography after TAVR, and a 63% reduction in hypo-attenuated leaflet thickening (HALT) per cardiac CT at 3 months, he reported at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics annual conference hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation, with study results simultaneously published in JAMA Cardiology.

"However, what we don't know to date is if this also translates into longer valve durability and ultimately better clinical long-term outcomes. This remains to be investigated," Autherith cautioned during a press conference.

Even so, the "really impressive" lowering of HALT in particular was highlighted by Adnan Chhatriwalla, MD, of Saint Luke's Mid America Heart Institute in Kansas City, Missouri. Considering the lower PVL as well, "these data suggest that we should routinely do [postdilation]," Chhatriwalla commented during the press conference.

In TAVR, postdilation is the controversial step of reinflating the balloon a second time inside the newly deployed THV, giving it a so-called "double tap" that in theory covers the operator's bases for optimizing THV geometry in the absence of a good way to gauge device expansion. If left alone, asymmetric device expansion may be associated with higher residual gradients, PVL, and impaired THV performance.

Safety is a major concern with postdilation, however, especially when it comes to possible annulus rupture, valve migration, and conduction system disruption.

"So you don't want to take it for no reason," said Susheel Kodali, MD, of NYU Langone Health in New York City, another panelist at TCT.

Kodali said that echocardiographic and fluoroscopic characteristics will be key to defining who gets TAVR with postdilation. He also cited predilation and longer balloon inflation as other strategies for optimizing THV valve expansion -- which is really the ultimate goal for the patient.

"It's valve expansion to the maximum that's needed for that patient, and that's where AI [artificial intelligence], echo, fluoro, all of these things are going to help us understand who to do [postdilation] in," Kodali commented. Currently, "we just inflate, deflate, and don't assess how is the valve expanded. I think we need to be better at that."

Reassuringly, DUOTAP reported a favorable safety trend for routine postdilation, albeit without reaching a statistical difference. Procedural or early clinical adverse events at 30 days reached 24.3% with postdilation versus 31.1% with controls. A new conduction system disorder requiring pacemaker implantation was logged in 20.3% and 21.6% of patients, respectively.

"Certainly yes, there may be some consequences to universally doing a double tap. But having said that, we very clearly often will see asymmetric expansion," said Sammy Elmariah, MD, of UCSF Health in San Francisco. "Some individuals don't pursue it and don't postdilate. And so at least this gives us more motivation to at least, in a selective fashion, to start postdilating those valves and to really aim for symmetric expansion of the valve."

The single-blind, single-center trial enrolled people with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transfemoral TAVR with a Sapien balloon-expandable platform. Participants had to have no high-risk features on CT, no bicuspid aortic valves, and no valve-in-valve procedures, among other exclusion criteria.

Investigators randomized 148 TAVR patients 1:1 to postdilation or no postdilation.

Autherith noted that this was a typical TAVR cohort with a median age of 81 years, 47% women, and a EuroScore-II of 2.3%. The THV sizes chosen were a mix of 23 mm (29.0%), 26 mm (48.7%), and 29 mm (22.3%). A Sapien device with Resilia tissue was given to 42.6% of the group.

Fluoroscopic analysis indicated that postdilation corrects THV asymmetry by inducing valve height reduction on the outer curve of the device.

Postdilation consistently corrected asymmetry across prespecified subgroups including those by sex, THV size, and aortic valve calcification. Only on a post hoc exploratory analysis did a signal emerge that possibly people who got predilation did not have the same benefit of postdilation, according to Autherith.

"Regarding the subgroup analysis, these were only 11 patients receiving predilation, so confidence intervals were quite wide. I think it's difficult to interpret, but of course this is also an important consideration," he said during the press conference.

Other findings include postdilation being tied to increased Doppler velocity index and reduced residual trans-prosthetic gradients on echocardiography. Cardiac CTs also linked the intervention to valves with larger inflow and midframe areas, plus an increase in outflow area, at 3 months.

#5851. What Car Screams 'I'm Divorced'?

There are few bigger changes in a person's life than when they get divorced, which is probably why it's not too uncommon for a divorce to be rung in with the purchase of a new car — provided you didn't get taken to the cleaners by your spouse's far-superior lawyers. You've got a new life, new priorities and even a new way you'd like to have yourself represented to the world, and that idea is what brings me to today's question.

I want to know what car screams "I'm divorced!" What car lets everybody know that it didn't work out between you and the missus (or mister)? While technically, yes, any car can be a divorced person's car, that's really not what I'm looking for today. I want to know what car leaves zero doubt that someone has to sit separately from his ex-wife at school functions for fear that there could be an incident.

I'm not going to be too much of a stickler about the car you pick, either. It can be new or used, because classic cars definitely have an air of divorce about them, too, and so do cheap used cars — especially if divorce court didn't go your way.

For my pick for this question, I'm going with something new to keep it interesting. The answer to which car screams "I'm divorced!" is the Dodge Charger Sixpack R/T — the Hurricane inline-six-powered Dodge muscle car. Specifically, it has to be the two-door coupe, because you're only seeing the kids on weekends, anyway. Why do you need easy access to the rear seats? Exactly.

The car has everything the modern divorced man needs: throwback looks to a time when their hair wasn't thinning, a big enough trunk to hold the toys they're going to bribe their kids with, and even a reasonable starting price at $51,990, including destination. Add in the 420 horsepower it produces and the fact it'll do zero to 60 mph in 4.6 seconds (fast enough to outrun your demons and the alimony payments), and you've got a winner on your hands. Of course, you could always go for the more expensive Charger Sixpack Scat Pack, but court was never going to let you off the hook that easily, so you've got to save where you can.

Anyway, that's enough out of me. How about you all head on down below and let your fellow Jalops know what cars scream "I'm divorced"? As always, I'll love you more if you tell me why you made your pick.
